title: A clear opening
hookLine: We have given you a clear victory, an opening, after Hudaybiyyah (48:1)

lines: A TREATY THAT FELT LIKE LOSING.
cards: About fourteen hundred Muslims, by the reports, set out from Medina toward Mecca dressed as pilgrims, with animals for sacrifice and no intention of fighting.

The biographies place it in the sixth year after the move to Medina. They want to perform the lesser pilgrimage, the 'umrah. At Hudaybiyyah, at the edge of the sacred land, the Quraysh block the road.
What follows is a treaty that, to many of the Muslims there, felt like losing. And on the way home, a surah arrives calling it a victory.

teach.b: The terms, as the hadith and biographies report them: turn back this year, come next year instead. A truce of ten years.
Anyone who came from Mecca to the Muslims without permission would be sent back; anyone who went the other way would not.

Even the writing stung: the Meccan envoy refused the words Messenger of God, and the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ agreed to sign as Muhammad, son of 'Abdullah. 'Umar, by his own later account in Sahih al-Bukhari, went to the Prophet and asked: are we not in the right?
Why accept this? On the road back to Medina, Surah Al-Fath was revealed. Pickthall translates its first verse: "Lo! We have given thee (O Muhammad) a signal victory."

teach.h: FATH: AN OPENING, LIKE A DOOR.
teach.b: The Arabic word is fath, and its first meaning is opening, like a door. Fath mubin: a clear opening. Bukhari records the Prophet saying a surah had come to him that night dearer to him than everything the sun rises upon.
How could a treaty like that be an opening?

The truce meant people could travel, trade and talk freely. Ibn Ishaq passes on the view of al-Zuhri, an early historian, that more people entered Islam in the two years after the truce than in all the years before.

The biographies tell how the next year the pilgrimage happened peacefully, and how within two years Mecca itself opened, almost without a fight. The companions who'd felt defeated came to see Hudaybiyyah as the hinge.
The surah didn't change the terms. It changed what they were looking at: not the door that closed, but the one that was opening.

how: Muslims retell Hudaybiyyah as a lesson in patience and trust, and many recite Surah Al-Fath when hoping for a way through a hard situation.

o: a clear opening, a closing that became a door
a peace treaty signed on equal, fair terms
a battle won outright by force of arms

p: the lesser pilgrimage they set out for
asked: are we not in the right?

s: Surah Al-Fath was revealed after a great battle victory
it came on the road home from a treaty many felt was a loss.
like a door; fath mubin is a clear opening.
the Prophet signed the treaty without the title Messenger of God
the Meccan envoy refused it, and he agreed to sign as son of 'Abdullah.

games.q: you are at Hudaybiyyah. the terms send you home without the pilgrimage. what does the surah revealed on the way back call it?
games.why: 48:1 calls it fath mubin. the truce opened the roads, and Mecca opened within two years.

practice: Bring to mind a door that closed on you: a job you didn't get, a plan that fell through, a no you're still sore about.

Don't rush to make it good; just hold it, then ask gently whether anything became possible because of it, a road, a person, a quiet. If nothing yet, that's honest too, and if you pray, you can ask to see the opening.

wordCard.voice: Fath mubin: the name 48:1 gives the treaty of Hudaybiyyah, a closing that turned out to be a door. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a clear opening, a manifest victory (48:1).

carryVoice: Your line: an opening. A closed door isn't always the end of the road. Day five hundred eighty, done.
